steps.label: KP04 Bayesian inference and maximum entropy | Guided study
01 · Keep the posterior to retain parameter uncertainty · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Female: Used on this page: noise variance 1, prior μ N(0,10), and N=2, x=2.

What do we retain with the whole curve?

steps.label: 01 · Keep the posterior to retain parameter uncertainty · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: p( X) p(X)p(); every candidate parameter carries a weight.

steps.label: 01 · Keep the posterior to retain parameter uncertainty · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: The width expresses uncertainty that the peak alone cannot describe.

steps.label: 02 · More observations concentrate the posterior · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Male: Used on this page: prior  N(0,10), noise variance 1, mean  x=2; vary only sample size N.

How does the distribution narrow with more data?

steps.label: 02 · More observations concentrate the posterior · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: μ_N=20N/(10N+1) and σ_N^2=10/(10N+1); the mean approaches the data mean while variance shrinks.

steps.label: 02 · More observations concentrate the posterior · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: More data gives a more concentrated belief, not merely another point estimate.

steps.label: 03 · Prediction includes both noise and parameter uncertainty · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Female: Used on this page: at N=2, noise variance σ^2=1 and posterior variance σ_N^2=0.4762.

Where does the extra variance come from?

steps.label: 03 · Prediction includes both noise and parameter uncertainty · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: Var(x X)=σ^2+σ_N^2=1.4762; posterior and predictive SDs are different.

steps.label: 03 · Prediction includes both noise and parameter uncertainty · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: Knowing the center more precisely does not remove the randomness of new observations.

steps.label: 04 · The predictive density widens when the center is uncertain · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Male: Used on this page: mean 1.9048, plug-in variance 1, and predictive variance 1.4762.

Why is the predictive peak lower?

steps.label: 04 · The predictive density widens when the center is uncertain · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: p(x X)= p(x)p( X)d weights parameters without changing the assumed sample noise.

steps.label: 04 · The predictive density widens when the center is uncertain · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: Ignoring parameter uncertainty can make predictions overconfident.

steps.label: 05 · More data brings point and Bayesian results closer · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Female: Used on this page: prior  N(0,10), noise variance 1, and fixed data mean 2.

Do the estimates approach each other with more data?

steps.label: 05 · More data brings point and Bayesian results closer · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: The mean and mode coincide for this Gaussian posterior. As σ_N^20, concentration makes a point approximation more reasonable.

steps.label: 05 · More data brings point and Bayesian results closer · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: Agreement under these conditions does not make the methods identical.

steps.label: 06 · On one support, a uniform density adds no preference · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Male: Used on this page: densities on [0,2], each with unit area; H=- p p, measured in nats.

Which choice adds the fewest shape assumptions?

steps.label: 06 · On one support, a uniform density adds no preference · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: With only the support constrained, uniform density attains H=2=0.6931.

steps.label: 06 · On one support, a uniform density adds no preference · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: Maximum entropy adds the least beyond the specified constraints.

steps.label: 07 · Support and unit area alone give a constant density · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Female: Used on this page: x[0,2], unit integral, and Lagrange multiplier .

What is height times interval width?

steps.label: 07 · Support and unit area alone give a constant density · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: The variational condition  p=-1 makes the density constant; normalization gives p=1/2 and =1-2.

steps.label: 07 · Support and unit area alone give a constant density · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: Uniformity follows because no location has an information advantage.

steps.label: 08 · Different constraints select different maximum-entropy families · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Male: Used on this page: maximum entropy requires a support and known moments; μ is the mean and σ^2 the variance.

Does adding a constraint preserve the solution?

steps.label: 08 · Different constraints select different maximum-entropy families · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: Uniform: H=(b-a); exponential: H=1+μ; Gaussian: H=12(2 eσ^2).

steps.label: 08 · Different constraints select different maximum-entropy families · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: Entropy values from different supports and constraints are not direct rankings of validity.

steps.label: 09 · Practice: posterior and predictive uncertainty · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Female: Used on this page: σ^2=2, prior  N(0,10), N=4, data mean 3, and unknown mean.

Find the center, then distinguish the variances.

steps.label: 09 · Practice: posterior and predictive uncertainty · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: Posterior precision is 1/10+4/2; its mean is (4·3/2)/(1/10+4/2); prediction adds variance 2.

steps.label: 09 · Practice: posterior and predictive uncertainty · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: Greater parameter certainty does not remove observation noise.

steps.label: 10 · Too few quadrature nodes can distort the predictive peak · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Male: Used on this page: posterior  N(1.9048,0.4762), noise variance 1, and 4 versus 15 quadrature nodes.

Can fewer quadrature nodes change the peak?

steps.label: 10 · Too few quadrature nodes can distort the predictive peak · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: Four nodes underestimate the center peak here; the direction depends on the integral and quadrature, not node count alone.

steps.label: 10 · Too few quadrature nodes can distort the predictive peak · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: Numerical integration accuracy must be checked for the actual setting.

steps.label: 11 · Practice: do not invent a peak from a support alone · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Female: Used on this page: support [0,3], no mean or location information, and unit total area.

How do height and entropy change with range?

steps.label: 11 · Practice: do not invent a peak from a support alone · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: No location has an added distinction, so the variational solution is constant; unit area fixes its height.

steps.label: 11 · Practice: do not invent a peak from a support alone · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: Being least committal means leaving unknown distinctions unknown.

steps.label: 12 · Retain uncertainty before choosing model complexity · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Male: Used on this page: posterior parameter uncertainty, posterior-weighted prediction, and maximum entropy under specified constraints.

What determines uncertainty and shape?

steps.label: 12 · Retain uncertainty before choosing model complexity · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: Point estimates, posteriors and maximum entropy answer different questions; multiple groups may also require a different density model.

steps.label: 12 · Retain uncertainty before choosing model complexity · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: Uncertainty and distribution shape are complementary modeling choices.
